title: The self-organized vacancy order in Pr$_9$Ge$_{16}$
authors: Jayashani S. T. Wickramasinghe, Melissa G. Anderson, Kelci Graville, Gregory T. McCandless, Zachary J. Morgan, Brianna R. Billingsley, Tai Kong, Hyunsoo Kim, Aleksandr V. Chernatyskiy, Simon G. Mitchell, Liang Wu, Julia Y. Chan, Feng Ye, Halyna Hodovanets
abstract: In this work, we report the discovery of a new crystal structure on the Ge-rich side of the Pr-Ge binary phase diagram. Using a high-temperature flux technique, we grew single crystals of $Pr_9Ge_{16}$, which adopt a previously unreported orthorhombic $Fdd$2 structure type featuring ordered Ge vacancies. We present the anisotropic magnetic properties and identify the crystallographic $b$ axis perpendicular to the crystal plane as the magnetic easy axis. Temperature-dependent resistivity measurements reveal metallic behavior with a distinct anomaly at $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ = 14.3 K. Hall resistivity data indicate that electron-like carriers dominate, with a carrier concentration on the order of $10^{27}~\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. The magnetic order is readily suppressed by a magnetic field of approximately 0.4 T applied along the easy $b$ axis.
summary: This work reports the discovery of a new crystalline phase, $	ext{Pr}_9	ext{Ge}_{16}$, which exhibits ordered vacancies within its structure. Electrically, it behaves as a metal with electron-like carriers, and magnetically, it displays an anisotropic magnetic order that can be suppressed by a small external field.
main_problem: The study reports the discovery of a new crystal structure ($	ext{Pr}_9	ext{Ge}_{16}$) and characterizes its complex physical properties, including magnetic and electronic behavior.
main_result: Single crystals were grown adopting an orthorhombic $Fdd2$ structure with ordered Ge vacancies. The material exhibits metallic conduction, electron-like carriers ($n \sim 10^{27} 	ext{ m}^{-3}$), and a magnetic transition at $T_C = 14.3 	ext{ K}$.
method: The research employed single crystal growth (high-temperature flux), structural characterization via XRD/Neutron Diffraction, and transport measurements (resistivity, Hall effect) alongside magnetization studies.
model_or_system: The physical system is the rare earth germanide $	ext{Pr}_9	ext{Ge}_{16}$. The electronic structure analysis suggests that the non-Kramers $	ext{Pr}^{3+}$ ion's $J=4$ ground state splits into nine singlet states due to low site symmetry.
key_observables: Anisotropic magnetization (easy axis along $b$), resistivity anomaly at $14.3 	ext{ K}$, Hall carrier concentration ($10^{27} 	ext{ m}^{-3}$), and satellite reflections indicating vacancy ordering.
important_parameters: Magnetic field required to suppress order ($\approx 0.4 	ext{ T}$); Carrier concentration ($n \sim 10^{27} 	ext{ m}^{-3}$); Transition temperature ($T_C = 14.3 	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The authors assume the structure is best described by the $Fdd2$ space group, despite discrepancies with published patterns; analysis of electronic properties relies on fitting Hall data to a one-band model.
figures_summary: Figures show powder XRD patterns comparing observed data to proposed structures ($I4_1/amd$ vs. $Fdd2$), and phase diagrams mapping magnetic order versus temperature and field.
paper_structure: The paper follows a progression from structural discovery (new $Fdd2$ structure with vacancy ordering) to electronic characterization (metallic behavior, electron carriers), culminating in the detailed analysis of anisotropic magnetic properties and phase transitions.
why_interesting: While primarily experimental, the investigation into the interplay between crystal lattice distortion (vacancy ordering) and emergent magnetic/electronic states is central to strongly correlated electron physics. The comparison to topological semimetals suggests potential avenues for studying exotic quantum phases in these materials.
